name: Assumptions for the Convergence

body_md:
The $L^\infty(\Omega)^d$ norm inherited from the solution space, in which the convergence is therefore naturally stated in, causes the Assumptions \ref{ass:numconv} to be rather restrictive. Material parameters need to be sufficiently regular and the convergence of the numerical input data is required in the $C^0([0,T], L^\infty(\Omega)^d)$ or $L^\infty(\Omega)^d$ norm, respectively.\par
    In particular, if the input data is not continuous, the discontinuities have to lie within the closure of all boundaries of the discrete elements $\Omega_i$ for all $\kappa_n$ in the chosen sequence $\kappa_n\searrow 0$, imposing significant geometrical restriction on the discontinuity set. The offset $\vec{o}_\kappa$ as introduced in Definition \ref{def:constdisc} can be used to mitigate this issue for simple discontinuity sets in the input data, as we will do in the numerical example shown in Section \ref{sect:numex}. This is nonetheless undesirable, and alternatives trying to evade the $L^\infty(\Omega)^d$ norm altogether are discussed in Remark \ref{rm:abouttheassumptionspt2}.\par
    Continuous input data however does not pose a problem for most choices of deriving the numerical input data $\vec{u}_0, \vec{v}_0, \vec{\mathbf{b}}_{\kappa}$ from the continuous $u_0, v_0, \mathbf{b}$ such as choosing the value at the index $i \in I^\kappa$ to be the value of the continuous input data at $x_i$, i.e. for example $(\vec{u}_0)_i = u_0(x_i)$, or the projection of the continuous input data under $\mathcal{P}_\kappa$. Lipschitz continuity of the input data would then result in a linear convergence of the discrete input data to the continuous one. \par
    This approach for choosing the numeric input data however requires careful handling of elements $\Omega_i$ with $x_i \not\in \Omega$. The solution for this is to continuously extend the input data to $\overline{B_{r}(\Omega)} := \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d: \text{dist}(x, \Omega)\leq r\}$ for a sufficiently chosen $r > \sqrt{d}\kappa/2$.

label: rm:DiscrConv
body_md:
\label{rm:DiscrConv} Proposition \ref{prop:contcontsol} explains the convergence result given in Theorem \ref{theo:convsemidiscr}, as all discontinuities present in the final solution have to be already present in the input data. This on the other hand requires the discontinuities in the input data to lie inside the closure of boundaries of all discrete elements $\Omega_i$ for all $\kappa_n$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$ in a given sequence of $\kappa_n \searrow 0$. This is enforced by the strict convergence requirements
\begin{equation*}
    \|\mathcal{K}_\kappa\vec{\mathbf{b}}_\kappa - \mathbf{b}\|_{C^0([0,T], L^\infty(\Omega)^d)}\searrow 0,\  \|v_0 - \mathcal{K}_\kappa \vec{v}_0^\kappa\|_{ L^\infty(\Omega)^d}\searrow 0,\  \|u_0 - \mathcal{K}_\kappa \vec{u}_0^\kappa\|_{ L^\infty(\Omega)^d} \searrow 0.
\end{equation*}
Proposition \ref{prop:contcontsol} indicates that fracture within the bulk appears not as a true discontinuity but rather as a steep but continuous function. In this sense, the model can be understood as a regular approximation of a truly discontinuous fracture model. Note that the horizon $\delta>0$ affects the bounds (\ref{eqn:fingroenregcontsol}) directly, such that they diverge as $\delta \searrow 0$. This would allow the displacement to become steeper as $\delta \searrow 0$. 
We do not claim the convergence of the peridynamic model to a sharp discontinuity model as $\delta \searrow 0$, but merely state that the practically observed localization of damage as $\delta\searrow 0$, which necessarily implies a steeper displacement in the presence of continuity is consistent with the bounds given here. \par
This interpretation is consistent with other works drawing parallels with phase-field approaches, interpreting other peridynamic-type models as hybrid phase-field type models with length parameter $\delta>0$ and a damage field whose evolution follows from the constitutive law (e.g. \cite{COSKUN2025106302, bromley2026blendedapproachevolvingphase}).

label: lemm:alt34weights
head: environment
name: Uniform Bounds on Discrete Integrals with Partial Area Weights

title: Proof
body_md:
We deal with these proofs by using the Assumptions \ref{ass:quadweights}, more precisely, the fact that $\omega^{ij}_\delta$ and $\omega_\delta(\|x_j-x_i\|_2)$ can only differ on the volume $B_{\delta + \sqrt{d}\kappa}(x_i)\backslash B_{\delta - \sqrt{d}\kappa}(x_i)$. This follows as the only $\Omega_j$ on which the values differ must fulfill $ \delta + \sqrt{d}/2\kappa \geq \|x_i-x_j\|_2 \geq \delta - \sqrt{d}/2\kappa$, therefore $\Omega_j \subset B_{\delta + \sqrt{d}\kappa}(x_i)\backslash B_{\delta - \sqrt{d}\kappa}(x_i)$ due to $\operatorname{diam}(B_j) = \sqrt{d}\kappa$. We then obtain
\begin{align*}
    &\Bigg|\sum_{j\not=i} \int_{\Omega_j}\frac{\omega_\delta^{ij}}{\|x'-x\|_2} \ \mathbf{d} x' - \sum_{j\not=i} \int_{\Omega_j}\frac{\omega_\delta(\|x_i-x_j\|_2)}{\|x'-x\|_2} \ \mathbf{d} x'\Bigg| \\
    &\leq \omega_\delta(\delta - 
\sqrt{d}\kappa) \operatorname{vol}(B_{\delta + \sqrt{d}\kappa}(0)\backslash B_{\delta - \sqrt{d}\kappa}(0)) \frac{1}{\delta - \sqrt{d}\kappa} \xrightarrow[]{\kappa \searrow 0} 0,
\end{align*}
independently of $i\in I^\kappa$.
The convergence follows from the fact that $\omega_\delta$ is non-increasing and finite on $(0,\delta]$. Using the triangle inequality and Lemma \ref{lemm:unifbndinteg}, yields the claim. \par
The other integral follows similarly, as again, (2) of Assumptions \ref{ass:quadweights} implies that if $w^{ij}$ and $\omega_\delta(\|x_i-x_j\|_2)$ differ, then $\|x_i-x_j\|\geq \delta - \sqrt{d}\kappa/2$.

name: Error Bound on the Discrete Weighting Function with Partial Area Weights

title: Proof
body_md:
We use a similar argument as in Lemma \ref{lemm:alt34weights}, reducing the argument to bounding the error term 
    \begin{align*}
        &\sum_{i\not=j}\int_{\Omega_j} |\omega_\delta^{ij}-\omega_\delta(\|x_j-x_i\|_2)| \ \mathbf{d} x' \\
        &\leq \omega_\delta(\delta - 
\sqrt{d}\kappa) \operatorname{vol}(B_{\delta + \sqrt{d}\kappa}(0)\backslash B_{\delta - \sqrt{d}\kappa}(0))  \in O(\kappa)
    \end{align*}
    The claim now follows from the triangle inequality and Lemma \ref{lemm:discrweighterrbnd}.
